content.thinking:
I'm putting together a careful postmortem and working out what goes in it. The alert says shopper totals don't reconcile, so I'm checking whether any shopper actually saw an error; the record doesn't show one, and I'm noting that the error rate was never measured.

I'm weighing how to word the symptom for the postmortem, since I can't tell whether shoppers actually saw anything wrong. The integrity check found stored spend totals that fell short of their purchases, so I'll phrase it that way rather than claim users noticed.

I'm working out the causal chain for the postmortem, tracing from the reconciliation mismatch back toward the flag that was switched on and the derive path that never writes the monthly total.

I'm now setting out the causal chain, starting from the symptom and working down toward the switch that caused it, and noting that the stored monthly totals stayed put while purchases kept coming in.

I'm checking whether any purchases since the onset would have been missed, and noting that the first affected purchase came after the feature flag was switched on, with no earlier deploy found in the window I read.

I'm settling on the last part of the postmortem: the ruled-out list stays empty, and I'm stating in that step that no earlier change was ruled out because the record has no metrics from before the onset, and that no deploy came back for the window I read. The fourth step says that with the flag on, purchases go through the derive path, which doesn't write the monthly total. That makes four steps, and I'm now turning to the root cause sentence.

I'm checking the wording of the root cause against what the record actually shows, and it rests on a single reading of the purchase path rather than a run. The likely mechanism is that once the setting was switched on, purchases were recorded without moving each shopper's stored running total for the month, so those totals fell behind what they had bought. I'm also noting that the totals already short will stay wrong and keep slipping while the setting stays on.

I'm drafting the contributing factors now, starting with the spend-integrity check that only runs every few days, which is why the fault stayed hidden for so long.

I'm drafting the second contributing factor: nothing I've seen shows a test of the flag-on path writing the month total before the flag went live. The fix would be to require a reconciliation run on that path before any such flag is turned on in production.

I'm drafting the action items now, starting with a detection step: running the spend reconciliation far more often than every few days, perhaps hourly, so a mismatch like this surfaces much sooner.

I'm listing the action items now: running the spend reconciliation on a much shorter schedule so mismatches surface sooner, adding a pre-enable check that tests both purchase paths before a flag like this goes live, and routing the spend-mismatch alert to on-call paging. I'm also planning a repair run of the monthly totals script, first as a dry run to review, then applied once the fix is in.

I'm weighing whether the action items should include a repair of the stored totals, and whether it has to wait until the fix is merged or the flag is reverted, so that the totals don't drift again while it runs. I'm also considering a separate check of November totals if the repair ends up running after the month turns over.

I'm weighing whether the repair should also cover monthly statements that may have gone out with short totals, and whether to check if any were sent since the onset.

I'm filling in the lessons section now, starting with what went well: the investigator anchored the timeline at the onset and found the flag change, and the on-call agent held off on the revert and left that call to a person. Code-Fix Agent also put a proposed fix up as draft pull request #572.

I'm weighing whether to treat the missing page as a contributing factor or as its own finding in what went wrong, since it didn't clearly shorten the time from onset to alert. I'm leaning toward listing it under what went wrong, because the on-call setup was already in place before the incident and nobody being paged only mattered once the revert was waiting on a person.

I'm checking the remaining lessons-learned items: nothing in the record shows a customer loss, but that's about the kind of fault, not luck, so I'm leaving that section empty. I'm also noting that the link from the flag to the stored totals rests on timing and Code-Fix's reading, and I'm about to test whether all the checked totals fell short in the same direction.

I'm checking the last stretch of the postmortem's wording: the figures I'm avoiding in prose, and the claim that the oldest affected purchase came after the onset. I'm also noting which assumptions the record can't support, such as whether statements and averages read the same stored field.

I'm working out how to date the change from the instant the flag was flipped, and I'm keeping the ruled-out list empty: no earlier change was ruled out, since the record has no metrics from before the onset and the window I searched held only this one change. For the second step, I'm stating that the stored month total stopped growing as purchases were recorded, so it fell below the sum of that shopper's purchases for the month, which is what the reconciliation compares against. Then I'll write the third step on the change itself and the fourth on why that change broke the totals.

I'm settling the symptom step and the flag-on mechanism, with the stored total not growing as purchases are recorded, falling behind what the shopper bought, and the change itself as the trigger.

action_items.item: Run the monthly-total reconciliation (`reconcile_monthly_totals`) on a much shorter schedule than the current spend-integrity check, so short totals are found soon after they start.

Before any feature flag that switches how purchases are recorded is turned on in production, require tests that record purchases through both the flag-on and flag-off paths and confirm the stored totals reconcile with the purchases.
Link the SpendTotalsDoNotReconcile alert to an on-call paging policy so that a person is paged when it fires.

Once the flag is reverted or the fix is merged, run `src/io_shop/repair_monthly_totals.py` as a dry run, review the accounts it plans to fix, then run it with `apply=True`, supplying a loader and saver for production storage.
Look into the accounts the repair script lists as having month totals above their purchases, which it leaves unchanged.
If the repair runs after November has ended, check and correct the November month totals separately, since the script covers only the current month.
Find out whether any monthly statements or spend averages shown to shoppers since the onset were built from short month totals, and decide whether to correct them for those shoppers.

causal_chain.step: The stored spend totals of the shoppers checked no longer matched the purchases behind them, falling short of what had been bought, starting from purchases recorded at the onset.
A shopper's stored month total did not grow as their purchases were recorded, so it fell below the sum of their this-month purchase prices, which is what the reconciliation compares it with.

Purchases began going through a different recording path when admin switched on the feature flag monthly-spend-feature at {P1.1}, shortly before the oldest affected purchase. No deploy came back for the window searched. No earlier change was ruled out: no metrics from before the onset were read, and nothing else in the record shows the service healthy with an earlier change in place.
With the flag on, purchases are recorded through a path that, by Code-Fix's reading, does not update the stored month total.

input.cause_in_plain_words: After a feature setting was switched on, the shop likely began recording each purchase without adding it to the shopper's stored running total for the month, so those stored totals fell behind what shoppers had actually bought.

contributing_factors.factor: The spend-integrity check that found the fault runs only every {A5} days, and no other check comparing stored month totals with purchases was seen.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: A check run much more often would have caught the short totals soon after the flag went on. Fewer purchases would have been recorded against wrong totals, and fewer totals would have been wrong.
contributing_factors.label: CF-1

contributing_factors.factor: Before monthly-spend-feature was switched on, no test or check was seen confirming that the flag-on purchase path keeps the stored month total in line with the purchases. By Code-Fix's account, the derive-path cases it adds would fail against the old code.
contributing_factors.had_it_been_otherwise: The flag-on path's failure to write the month total would have been found before the flag reached production, and the flag would not have been switched on with it.
contributing_factors.label: CF-2

went_well.item: The Investigator Agent placed the start of the incident at the oldest affected purchase rather than at the alert.
Argus read the flag provider's history and found the switch of monthly-spend-feature just before the onset.
Argus did not revert the flag itself, since nothing would show whether the revert worked within the time it waits, and left the revert to a person as a recommendation.
The Code-Fix Agent proposed a fix and a one-off repair script as draft pull request #572.

went_wrong: Nobody was paged: the alert was linked to no on-call incident, so the recommended revert and the repair waited on someone noticing.

input.root_cause: With monthly-spend-feature on, `record_a_purchase` in `src/io_shop/purchase_ledger.py` records each purchase through `record_purchase_deriving_the_month`, which adds the purchase to `purchases` and moves `total_cents` but never writes `total_this_month_cents`. Each shopper's stored month total therefore stays where it was while their this-month purchases grow, and falls further below their sum with every purchase.
input.still_at_risk: While monthly-spend-feature stayed on, shoppers' stored month totals could keep falling further behind with every purchase, the totals already short stay wrong until someone rewrites them, and the monthly statements and per-item spend averages that read those totals could show shoppers the wrong figures.
input.symptom: Shoppers' stored spend totals fell short of the purchases behind them
